EQ_CURVE_GRID.doc: The log frequency grid an EQ response curve is sampled on: point k is startHz x 10^(k / pointsPerDecade), for k = 0, 1, 2 and on while the point is at or below nyquistFraction x the rate / 2. At these values the points up to 20 kHz are the 160 points from 20 Hz to 20 kHz the console draws its EQ curve on, the same at every rate whose bound lies above 20 kHz; above 20 kHz the grid goes on at the same step up to the bound.

docs.startHz: the first point of the grid, in Hz
docs.pointsPerDecade: the points in each decade; neighbouring points are a ratio of 10^(1 / pointsPerDecade) apart
docs.nyquistFraction: the last point is the last at or below this fraction of the Nyquist frequency (the rate / 2)

EQ_HPF_ONS.doc: The HPF's switch: off, the filter is not in the EQ's bank at all; on, its one or two Butterworth sections run after the bands. It comes up off, on the console's channel EQ and in omx-dsp's EQ face (see EQ_PASS_FILTER_DEFAULTS).

HPF_FREQ_RANGE.doc: Where the HPF cutoff can sit (low end); mirrors the drawn low-frequency handle.

FILTER_SLOPES.doc: The pass-filter slopes the EQ offers, in dB per octave: the HPF's slope, and by use the LPF's. The id is the slope: 12 is one maximally flat section, 24 the two-section Butterworth.

EQ_LPF_ONS.doc: The LPF's switch: off, the filter is not in the EQ's bank at all; on, its one or two Butterworth sections run after the bands and the HPF. It comes up off, on the console's channel EQ and in omx-dsp's EQ face (see EQ_PASS_FILTER_DEFAULTS).

LPF_FREQ_RANGE.doc: Where the LPF cutoff can sit (high end).

EQ_BAND_TYPES.doc: The generic EQ band shapes, in the order a picker offers them and in the order of the integer a plugin host sees on a band type port. The id is the name; the position is the value. A bell is the shape a band added by the operator starts as.

EQ_FREQ_RANGE.doc: The frequency band a parametric band can be dragged across.

EQ_GAIN_RANGE.doc: The parametric-band gain travel, in dB. The ± scalar `clampEqGain` enforces is READ off this (the engine derives its gain limit from `max`), so the bound is stated once and a surface cannot draw a wider knob than the clamp will honour.

EQ_Q_RANGE.doc: The Q (resonance) extent of a parametric band.

EQ_NOTCH_Q_RANGE.doc: The Q extent of a NOTCH band. Wider than EQ_Q_RANGE on purpose (#116, operator decision): an ultra-narrow surgical cut is the notch shape's whole point — the FBS ring-out pool plants dbx-AFS-style ring killers at Q ≈ 116 (~1/80 octave), inaudible on program yet fatal to a single ringing frequency. Gain-carrying shapes stay bounded at EQ_Q_RANGE — a Q-116 bell is a resonator, not an EQ move.

EQ_BAND_ONS.doc: A band's switch. Off, the band is not in the EQ's bank (the slots close up); on, it runs, parked when it is a gain-carrying shape at 0 dB. A band comes up off (operator ruling, 2026-10-13): an omx-eq plugin brings every band up off so a racked instance is a wire, and the console's channel EQ reads its come-up value here. A stored session keeps its own band states; only a fresh band comes up off.

EQ_MAX_BANDS.doc: The maximum number of parametric bands a channel EQ may hold — the operator can add up to this many. Generated into `omx_contract_limits.h` as `OMX_EQ_MAX_BANDS`, which `omx_biquad.h` reads (the engine's conformance test reads the header): the native lane allocates exactly this many biquad slots per channel and silently clamps above it, so the model, the wire, and the DSP agree by test, not by memory.

ISO_THIRD_OCTAVE_CENTRES_HZ.doc: The standard ISO 266 one-third-octave centre frequencies, 20 Hz–20 kHz (31 bands) — the classic 31-band graphic-EQ layout's centres.

GEQ_BANDS.doc: The graphic EQ's section count: DERIVED from ISO_THIRD_OCTAVE_CENTRES_HZ, never a second literal. Generated into `omx_contract_limits.h` as `OMX_GEQ_BANDS`, which sizes `mix_geq.h`'s section array — its OWN budget, never a claimant on EQ_MAX_BANDS (roster ruling 3).

OPERATOR_EQ_BANDS_RESERVE.doc: The band slots kept for the operator's own hand: the reserve the feedback suppressor and the ring correction may never eat into. Nine is the working set a live EQ actually holds. The budget OPERATOR_EQ_BANDS_RESERVE + FBS_DEFAULT_MAX_AUTO_BANDS + HRP_DEFAULT_MAX_AUTO_BANDS (9 + 6 + 8 = 23) must fit EQ_MAX_BANDS, and `omx-contract validate` refuses data where it does not.

EQ_BAND_COUNTS.doc: How many bands each strip type's EQ starts with (`default`) and may hold (`max`). `channel` is the console's channel strip: it starts with four and the operator adds bands up to EQ_MAX_BANDS (a band added takes the frequency it is added at, so no default is declared for it). `strip` is the omx-strip plugin's EQ and `eq8`, `eq16` and `eq32` the omx-eq plugins, whose bands are fixed. A default may never exceed its maximum, and the default centres of any count come from the one default rule, whatever the strip.

EQ_BAND_DEFAULTS.doc: What every band of a fresh EQ comes up at, whatever its type and its strip: flat (0 dB) and Q 1. The band frequencies and types come from the default rule.

EQ_PASS_FILTER_DEFAULTS.doc: The corners the high-pass and low-pass filters of a fresh EQ are parked at, whatever the strip. Both come up off.

EQ_DEFAULT_CENTRES_FOUR_BAND_HZ.doc: The default band centres of a four-band EQ, Hz: ISO 266 preferred values, two to two and a half octaves apart. The default rule gives every other band count its centres from the preferred series; four bands start here.

EQ_CENTRE_SERIES_R20_HZ.doc: The ISO 266 R20 preferred frequencies from 20 Hz to 20 kHz (61 values, sixth-octave spacing): the finer series the default band rule falls back to where R10 (ISO_THIRD_OCTAVE_CENTRES_HZ, 31 values) has too few to give every band its own centre. R10 is a subset of it.

LOWPASS_HANDOVER.doc: Where the low-pass section hands its poles over from the matched pair to the prewarped bilinear pair, as fractions of Nyquist, and how that band moves with Q. At `qHi` (1/sqrt(2), the 12 dB Butterworth) the band runs from `loAtHiQ` to `hiAtHiQ`; at `qLo` (0.5412, the low-Q half of the 24 dB Butterworth) and below, from `loAtLoQ` to `hiAtLoQ`; between the two it moves linearly. Above `qHi` the prototype peaks, and the band's end moves down to `hiAtPeakQ` by `qPeak`, held above it. Below the band the low-pass is the matched design unchanged.

FBS_AUTO_BANDS_RANGE.doc: The travel of the feedback suppressor's per-channel cap on the bands it plants: at least one, never more than the EQ itself holds. The ceiling is EQ_MAX_BANDS, read rather than re-typed: the suppressor plants its notches in the channel's own EQ, so a cap above the EQ's band count would promise bands that cannot exist. The come-up value is FBS_DEFAULT_MAX_AUTO_BANDS.

FBS_SENSITIVITY_RANGE.doc: The feedback detector's sensitivity travel: a 0..1 aggression scalar, stepped in twentieths because the operator sets it by feel during a ring-out, not by number. Not a surface position: the bounds coincide with a normalised position's, the step is what says they are different facts. The come-up value is FBS_DEFAULT_SENSITIVITY.

FBS_MERGE_CENTS_RANGE.doc: The same-ring merge radius, in cents: a confirmed find within this musical distance of a standing suppressor band is that band ringing again, a re-arm and never a new slot. A semitone (100) covers a drifting wedge mode; 0 keeps only the FFT-jitter floor. Steps of 10 cents.

FBS_COOLDOWN_MINUTES_RANGE.doc: The ring memory, in minutes: how long a fully released find's escalation survives, so a chronic ringer re-plants with its doubled holds instead of starting over. 0 disables the memory.

FBS_HOLD_SECONDS_RANGE.doc: The clean hold's finite travel, in seconds: a floor of 1 s (a hold of zero is not a hold) and a ceiling of five minutes, the longest an automatic notch is ever held. A notch kept for the whole show is the unbounded 'never' case, which is no number; this bounds only the number. The come-up value is FBS_DEFAULT_HOLD_SECONDS.

SUBHARMONIC_RADIUS_BINS.doc: How far (bins) around bin/2 and bin/3 PSHR (`omx_fbs_pshr`) scans for a sub-harmonic line. A true half/third partial lands mid-bin in the worst case (bin/2 and bin/3 are rarely integers) and spectral leakage smears it one bin further; ±2 covers both. Measured on the #116 live-music corpus: every false positive's sub-line sat inside this window. Deliberately NOT wider — at low bins the window is already a large fraction of an octave, and widening it would start reading unrelated program lines as "sub-harmonics" of real feedback.

FBS_PAPR_GUARD_BINS.doc: PAPR's guard band: bins either side of the peak left out of the floor average (its own skirt).

FBS_PNPR_RADIUS_BINS.doc: PNPR's neighbourhood radius in bins, and the guard inside it that belongs to the peak's own skirt: a pure tone is compared with bins 2 and 3 away on each side.

FBS_PNPR_GUARD_BINS.doc: The guard inside PNPR's neighbourhood radius that belongs to the peak's own skirt, in bins.

FBS_PHPR_HARMONICS.doc: How many harmonics PHPR reads above the candidate: 2f, 3f and 4f.

FBS_PSHR_SELF_SKIP_BINS.doc: PSHR skips sub-window bins within this many of the candidate, so a low bin never measures its own skirt as a sub-harmonic.

FBS_FLOOR_LIN.doc: The magnitude floor of every detector dB reading (−240 dB): a zero bin stays finite.

FBS_TRACK_SLOTS.doc: Tracked candidate bins per armed channel. A candidate that finds no free slot is COUNTED and reported, never dropped silently; the identity corpus peaks at 34.

PSHR_MIN_DB.doc: Minimum PSHR (`omx_fbs_pshr`) (dB) for a candidate frame to count as sub-harmonic-CLEAN. Evidence-set on the #116 corpus, margin on both sides: the four live false positives (musical overtones at 1 869.1 / 832.0 / 263.7 / 228.5 Hz) read PSHR between −10.2 and +8.8 dB across their windows — never a 5-frame sub-clean stretch, and the single closest approach (+8.8) is isolated between frames at ≈ −1 and −10 — while the committed #106 injected ramp reads ≥ +12.2 dB from its second frame on (its frame 0 sits at +9.4, costing exactly one frame of confirm latency, pinned in the corpus test). A static program line at f/2 of REAL feedback also clears this fast: the runaway gains several dB per hop on anything static, so the deferral is transient.

GROWTH_WINDOW_FRAMES.doc: How many of a candidate bin's most recent dB readings feed the growth-slope estimate (the engine's least-squares slope) — set equal to DEFAULT_THRESHOLDS's `persistFrames` so growth is judged over the SAME window persistence already demands (the full run since the bin became a candidate, not a shorter or longer slice of it). Long enough that a couple of noisy/vibrato frames can't fake a trend by themselves.

DEEP_PLATEAU_FRAMES.doc: The DEEP plateau tier's dwell: ~2 s at the watcher's 10 Hz — the TIME that buys the deeper floor its music safety (see DetectThresholds.deepPlateauFloorDb).

GROWTH_MIN_DB_PER_FRAME.doc: Minimum least-squares slope, in dB PER FRAME, over GROWTH_WINDOW_FRAMES for a bin to count as "running away" rather than merely holding level. Set with real margin on BOTH sides — comfortably above measurement jitter on a held tone or a quiet/broadband mix (well under 0.2 dB/frame in practice) and comfortably below a genuine feedback ramp, which climbs several dB across a handful of ~20 ms hops as it heads toward clipping. The acceptance bar is "arming must never burst-alarm on non-growing content", so this errs conservative (under-fire a marginal ramp) rather than tight (risk a false alarm) — the ramp gate (`omx_fbs_is_growing`) also requires the window's end to sit above its start, a cheap belt-and-braces check against a fit dragged positive by one mid-window wobble.

GROWTH_MAX_DIP_DB.doc: Largest single-frame DIP (dB) a run-away window may contain. Real feedback climbs every hop; a small allowance covers measurement jitter and the −0.3 dB-ish wobble frames seen on live captures, while any real drop (a note ending, tremolo) breaks the run.

GROWTH_MIN_TOTAL_RISE_DB.doc: Minimum END-TO-END rise (dB) across the window. The live-music corpus showed sustained melody notes drifting up ~4–5 dB over a window without ever being feedback; a loop past unity gains several dB per hop and clears 6 dB in a window trivially. Below this the tone is holding level, not running away.

GROWTH_MAX_SINGLE_FRAME_SHARE.doc: Cap on the share of the window's total rise a SINGLE frame may carry. Feedback is exponential in amplitude ⇒ linear in dB ⇒ its rise is distributed roughly evenly across the window; a musical attack / re-articulation puts almost the whole rise in one hop (the exact shape behind every one of the 72 live false positives of the live-music corpus). One half is generous to real ramps (an even N-frame ramp puts 1/(N−1) per hop) and fatal to steps. A side effect worth knowing: a 2-sample window can never pass (one hop IS the whole rise), so confirmation always rests on at least three frames of actual ramp evidence.

GROWTH_CONFIRM_FRAMES.doc: How many CONSECUTIVE frames the ramp gate (`omx_fbs_is_growing`) must hold before a bin confirms — the time-domain tiebreak for the one shape a single window cannot judge: a smooth musical crescendo. Within one window a +6 dB swell (live corpus: a C6 at 1 049 Hz, `[-53.7, -51.4, -50.4, -48, -47.3]`) is indistinguishable from slow feedback — the difference is only visible on the NEXT hop, where a crescendo peaks and plateaus (the window's rise collapses) while feedback keeps climbing. Requiring the gate to hold twice in a row costs a clean ramp nothing — its gate is already true while persistence is still arming — and blocks the swell that peaks the very frame it would have confirmed.

DEFAULT_THRESHOLDS.doc: The corpus-tuned SAFE DEFAULT — today's exact gates, assembled byte-for-byte from the exported consts above (which stay the authoritative literal source, so the corpus test's import type { MagnitudeSeries } from './spectrum-bands.js'; imports remain the single truth). This is the ANCHOR the whole sensitivity mapping pins to: thresholdsFor`(0, 'live')` and `(0, 'fixed')` both deep-equal this object, so an untouched channel runs the identical detector it does now. `plateauFloorDb` is omitted ⇒ the #140 plateau route is OFF at the default.

FBS_MAX_NOTCH_DEPTH_DB.doc: THE NOTCH DEPTH LAW: the deepest cut any machine planter may propose from one reading, in dB. A number, not a literal at the call site, because two planters now lean on it. FBS derives a candidate's depth from the peak-to-average ratio around its bin and stops here; Room Analysis derives a mode's depth from its height above the median curve and is held to the SAME ceiling (the room-analysis design — "never more than the FBS notch depth law"). Written twice as `18` those two bounds would be equal by coincidence and could drift apart in silence. It is a CEILING ON THE PROPOSAL, not the final gain: a band that lands as a rampable BELL is bounded again by `EQ_GAIN_RANGE`, which is tighter. A planter must honour both and REPORT when either bit, never quietly deliver a shallower cut than it was asked for.

FBS_DEFAULT_NOTCH_Q.doc: Default planted-notch width (Q) — the dbx-AFS-style ultra-narrow notch the corrector plants. `addBand`'s per-shape clamp holds it at 116 for a fixed notch and narrows it to 8 for a live bell, so this is the declared starting point rather than the width every notch ends up with.

FBS_DEFAULT_MAX_AUTO_BANDS.doc: Default per-channel cap on auto-planted bands — a full pool plants nothing and raises a pool-full alert instead (predictability over silent eviction).

FBS_DEFAULT_HOLD_SECONDS.doc: The clean hold a live notch comes up with before it lifts, in seconds. A live ring is usually a transient microphone and monitor geometry event, so the default notch is a short parachute, not a set-and-forget cut (the ring-out mode is for that). A surface may offer s, min and infinity; the value is always seconds.

FBS_DEFAULT_SENSITIVITY.doc: The detection sensitivity a channel comes up with, on FBS_SENSITIVITY_RANGE. 0 is the corpus-tuned gate set and the safe default: an untouched channel detects as one built before the control existed. Raising it shortens latency and relaxes prominence within music-safe bounds.

HRP_AMOUNT_RANGE.doc: How much of the computed correction HRP applies: 0 = analyse only, 1 = the full cut. It comes up at 0.5, half the computed cut.

HRP_AUTO_BANDS_RANGE.doc: The travel of HRP's per-channel cap on the bands it plants: at least one, never more than the EQ itself holds (EQ_MAX_BANDS). The come-up value is HRP_DEFAULT_MAX_AUTO_BANDS; a channel that needs more can have more, as an explicit decision with a visible cost.

HRP_MAX_CUT_DB.doc: The largest automatic cut HRP may place on one harmonic, as a POSITIVE dB magnitude. Well inside the ±15 dB an operator band may hold (core's `EQ_GAIN_LIMIT_DB`): an automatic correction the operator did not ask for gets far less authority than one they dialled themselves.

HRP_MAX_VOICES.doc: How many simultaneous musical voices the detector may report on one channel. PINNED to `OMX_HRP_MAX_VOICES` in `pipewire-native/src/hrp_pitch.h` — the C voice set is a FIXED-SIZE array, so a TS number above the macro promises voices the analyser structurally cannot return, and one below it silently drops notes the C already found. the engine's conformance test reads the header and holds the pair equal. EIGHT (operator sizing, 2026-09-01): a guitar sounds six strings, a piano or string-section voicing sits at eight. It is a SEARCH ceiling, not a cost — the detector abandons a round as soon as no credible candidate remains, so monophonic material costs what it always did.

HRP_FAMILY_SEARCH.doc: What each instrument family implies about the HRP search: `maxVoices`, how many notes the family can sound at once (the number its corrections are budgeted against), and `f0MinHz` to `f0MaxHz`, where its fundamentals can lie. Each is the widest the family can be, not the typical one: a range too narrow hides a note from the detector, one slightly too wide costs a few more sweep steps. One entry per INSTRUMENT_FAMILIES id; the confidence floor does not follow the family.

HRP_BAND_Q.doc: The Q of an HRP correction band — one declared number, operator-adjustable later. A musical cut, not a ring killer: FBS's default notch Q is ~116 because a howl is a single frequency, whereas a partial that is too loud is a note an instrument is playing and a surgical null on it would be heard as a hole. 5 sits mid-band in the 4…6 range a musical subtractive cut occupies, and inside EQ_Q_RANGE — the gain-carrying shapes' extent — so it survives the store's clamp unchanged. Deliberately NOT derived from the harmonic index. A derivation invented with no measurement behind it is a second declaration wearing a formula; this is revisited when the analyse-only surface shows what real corrections look like.

HRP_EXCESS_THRESHOLD_DB.doc: How far a partial must stand above its LEARNED BASELINE before HRP calls it a resonance (increment 8: `deviation = measured − baseline[note][harmonic]`). A partial level tells you nothing on its own; what marks a resonance is a partial louder than THIS instrument normally measures at THIS note. Three decibels is the same order as the feedback detector's peak-to-neighbour gate and for the same reason: below it, an ordinary performance's variation — a bow dug in, a verse sung harder — would be flattened, and flattening expression is not correcting a room. (Before the learned model existed this same threshold gated the placeholder neighbour rule; the number and its reasoning carried over.)

HRP_GAIN_STEP_DB.doc: How far ONE reconcile pass may move an HRP band's gain, in dB — the gain smoothing, done at the control level because the native cascade applies pushed coefficients verbatim and the design forbids interpolating there. An unbounded gain step is a waveform discontinuity — the click heard when a correction entered or left at full depth (found live, 2026-08-20, the evening increment 9 raised the enter/leave rate). Bounded, a correction ENTERS by deepening from silence and LEAVES by walking to exactly 0 dB — the provable parked identity (`eqBandIsIdentity`) — from which removal is bit-identical. Two decibels per pass at the corrector's 10 Hz cadence walks the full HRP_MAX_CUT_DB travel in ~300 ms: the same order as the tracker's stability hold and FBS's lift steps, while each individual move stays below audibility on a Q-5 bell.

HRP_COLLISION_CENTS.doc: How close two correction candidates must sit, in cents, to count as the SAME spectral region: within it, the stronger candidate is selected and the weaker discarded rather than two near-identical filters being planted. One semitone, and the number follows from HRP_BAND_Q: a Q-5 bell's −3 dB half-width is ~170 cents, so two cuts a semitone apart overlap over most of their travel — the second one deepens the first far more than it shapes anything of its own. The design makes the threshold configurable and tested: declared once here, a parameter everywhere below.

HRP_ATTRIBUTION_CENTS.doc: The ATTRIBUTION window: two partials closer than this are one spectral event as far as the desk can tell — the same ±1 bin `omx_hrp_bin_peak` reads over, expressed musically so it holds across the range. A different law from HRP_COLLISION_CENTS (the SELECTION window, which stays above it): this one is the analyser's resolution, that one the corrector's. Generated into `omx_contract_limits.h` as `OMX_HRP_ATTRIBUTION_CENTS`; `hrp_attribute.h` reads it.

HRP_DEFAULT_MAX_AUTO_BANDS.doc: How many bands HRP may plant on ONE channel — its half of the machine budget, and the number that makes the budget FORECASTABLE rather than emergent. Without it the count is whatever the material happens to provoke: the placement law is sparse, so a clean note plants two bands and a resonant room plants nine, and nobody can answer "will this fit?" until it does not. With FBS senior that discovery would happen at showtime, to the junior planter, silently. Declared instead, the whole sum is arithmetic an operator can read before a note is played: operator bands + FBS maxAutoBands + HRP maxAutoBands <= EQ_MAX_BANDS EIGHT — ONE CORRECTION PER VOICE at full polyphony (operator sizing, 2026-09-01). The detector's ceiling is HRP_MAX_VOICES voices, a guitar's six strings and a piano/string voicing's eight, and a budget below the voice count would decide by arithmetic which of the notes actually sounding may be corrected — a limit nobody could read off the desk. Scarcity is handled where it belongs instead: the candidates from every voice meet in ONE globally ranked list and the head of it is what gets planted. It is NOT a claim to seniority, and it is larger than FBS's six. Seniority is the ALLOCATION ORDER — `HrpPlanter` takes only `EQ_MAX_BANDS − others.length`, the remainder after the operator and every other machine — so a bigger junior default cannot reach a senior slot; it only means HRP asks for more of what is left. the engine's conformance test asserts both halves. The per-channel DEFAULT; the row's travel is HRP_AUTO_BANDS_RANGE, so a channel that needs more can have more, as an explicit decision with a visible cost.

HRP_HARMONIC_COUNT.doc: How many harmonics the HRP model tracks, H1 to H12: the partials it measures per voice. Not a band budget: the number it may cut is the channel's free EQ slots, which is smaller and belongs to the channel. omx-dsp's HRP analysis sizes its per-voice partial arrays by the same number (OMX_HRP_HARMONICS).

OUTPUT_DELAY_RANGE.doc: The per-destination output delay travel, the whole-sample delay a route leg or a bus output is aligned with (omx-dsp's omx_idelay.h). max is the delay ring's ceiling: 1000 ms is the live-console norm and a distance ceiling, about 343 m of throw. A surface that offered more than the ring holds would draw travel the DSP clamps away.

BUTTERWORTH_Q.doc: The Q of a second-order Butterworth section, 1/√2 — maximally flat, the one value every Butterworth biquad in the tree designs at: the LR4 crossover section, the pitch pre-filter and the drive's tilt / band / HF sections, in TS and (as `OMX_BUTTERWORTH_Q`) in C (§7, the scalar door).

ALLPASS_LIMITS.doc: The first-order all-pass section's contract tolerance. `unityTolerance` is the fraction of the larger side within which the block energy identity (the sum of y squared plus the pole times the end state squared equals the sum of x squared plus the pole times the start state squared) must hold, which is what makes the section unity magnitude. A design constant of the primitive, not a control: no row serves it.

XOVER_LIMITS.doc: The Linkwitz-Riley crossover primitives' numbers. `lr2SectionQ` is the Q of the one cookbook section an LR2 crossover runs per band (a squared first-order Butterworth, critically damped); `lr4SectionQ` is the Q of each of the two sections an LR4 crossover runs (a squared second-order Butterworth); `partitionTolerance` is the fraction of max(1, block peak) within which the low and high outputs must sum to the all-pass output. Measured worst case 9e-8. Design constants and tolerances, not controls.

FDELAY_MOD_READ_ORDER.doc: The order the chorus and flanger construct their lines with (four taps).

FDELAY_READ_L1_NORM.doc: `Λ` for the chorus/flanger read — ONE value; the header and every law read this.

GATE_CONTINUOUS_TRAVELS.doc: The gate's threshold, range, release and ratio as a plugin host draws them: GATE_LIMITS' bounds, units and defaults with no step. The console's row quantises these four to whole steps (1 dB, 10 ms, 1:1), and a travel whose step is 1 or more reads as an integer control; the omx-strip plugin has always offered them continuous, so it reads this table instead. Every number but the step is GATE_LIMITS', held equal by test/continuous-travels.test.mjs. Not rendered to C: no C reader needs a second spelling of the gate's bounds.

COMP_CONTINUOUS_TRAVELS.doc: The compressor's threshold and release as a plugin host draws them: COMP_LIMITS' bounds, units and defaults with no step. The console's row quantises them to whole steps (1 dB, 10 ms), and a travel whose step is 1 or more reads as an integer control; the omx-strip plugin has always offered them continuous, so it reads this table instead. Every number but the step is COMP_LIMITS', held equal by test/continuous-travels.test.mjs. Not rendered to C: no C reader needs a second spelling of the compressor's bounds.

PARAM_SCALES.doc: How a host draws a parameter: linear, logarithmic (a frequency, a time) or in discrete steps. The words omx-plugins' declarations and plugin-hostd's protocol use; a travel names its own with `scale`.

EQ_CONTINUOUS_TRAVELS.doc: The EQ's three frequency travels as a host draws them: the band frequency, the high-pass corner and the low-pass corner, EQ_FREQ_RANGE's, HPF_FREQ_RANGE's and LPF_FREQ_RANGE's bounds with no step and a logarithmic scale. The console's EQ quantises frequency to 10 Hz; a frequency drags continuously on a log axis, which is how every host draws it, so this is the form the omx-plugins read. Every number but the step is the source's, held equal by test/continuous-travels.test.mjs. Not rendered to C: no C reader needs a second spelling of the EQ's bounds.

READOUT_RATE_HZ.doc: How often a readout's value is published: 50 Hz, one value every 20 ms, the rate a host sends a moving meter at. Every readout reads it as its `rateHz` (docs/readouts.md).

BIQUAD_KINDS.doc: The biquad section kinds the EQ design builds, in the order of the integer a kernel reads: the bell, the two shelves, the pass filters, the notch, the bandpass (the de-esser's detector band, never an EQ band), and the first- and second-order allpasses (the dynamic EQ's and the phase tool's sections). The design itself is omx-dsp's `omx_eq_design`; the console draws its curves from a twin of it, and both dispatch on this list. No come-up id: a kind is chosen by the stage that designs the section.

INSTRUMENT_FAMILIES.doc: The instrument families a channel may be assigned, a broad prior and never an identification: HRP narrows where its detector looks for a fundamental and how many voices it looks for by the family (HRP_FAMILY_SEARCH), and nothing else. The order is the integer that crosses a port or a process boundary (omx-dsp's OmxHrpFamily, the HRP live face's family port). A channel with no family carries -1, which no id names, and the detector then runs its own wide defaults; so the set has no come-up id.

STANDARD_SAMPLE_RATES.doc: The standard sample rates (Hz) the desk recognises — the pro-audio superset. One source of truth for the clock controller's `clock.allowed-rates` seed, the force row's validation ceiling and the device-rate probe fallback. What the operator is OFFERED is always the DEVICE's own `supportedRates` — this is the ceiling a write is refused by, never a menu.

DSP_KNOB_REFERENCE_RATE.doc: The rate a unit-range DSP knob is quoted at (R-058): the rate this desk runs (ruling 2026-09-14). A kernel raises the knob to `REF / sr`, so at this rate the exponent is exactly 1 and the response is bit-for-bit the one cut before the law. Emitted to C as `OMX_DSP_KNOB_REFERENCE_RATE`; the reverb damping and FX-delay tone references `#define` from it.

ORACLE_FLOOR_RATES.doc: The four rates every kernel oracle runs at, whatever STANDARD_SAMPLE_RATES says: a declared list missing one of them stops a suite instead of testing less (omx-dsp, omx-plugins and omx-clap-host run their oracles at these).

RME_RATES.doc: The nine rates an RME interface clocks at, 32 to 192 kHz. STANDARD_SAMPLE_RATES is a subset of them; an oracle that runs here also covers 32, 64 and 128 kHz, where a kernel still has to meet its closed form even though the console never asks for them.
